title: The Importance of Participation
author: Bronwyn Ryrie Jones
summary: Bronwyn Ryrie Jones opens a three-part series on classroom participation by arguing that patchy participation - the near-universal complaint among teachers - is not a minor management annoyance but the central mechanism through which learning, explicit teaching, and inclusive classroom culture succeed or fail. Her core claim, grounded in Daniel Willingham's principle that what students think about determines what they learn, is that only students themselves can do the cognitive work of wrestling with curriculum content - teachers cannot learn for them, so participation rates directly gate learning. She argues participation is what makes explicit teaching actually possible: without students' responses to prompts and checks for understanding making their thinking visible, teachers 'are flying blind' and cannot teach responsively, regardless of how well-designed their explicit instruction is. Beyond cognition, Ryrie Jones connects participation to belonging (disengagement or a few students dominating both damage collective classroom culture) and to rehearsal (sustained participation over many lessons is what builds durable fluency, e.g., in verb conjugation). Her sharpest and most unsettling point closes the piece: students who participate more also receive disproportionately more feedback and encouragement from teachers, meaning the students who most need support - who tend to participate least - are systematically the ones who receive the least of it, making participation an equity issue as much as a pedagogical one.
points: Ryrie Jones's foundational claim, via Daniel Willingham: it is what students think about - not what teachers say - that determines lesson success, so because only students can do the cognitive work of engaging with content, participation rates directly gate learning.

Her argument that participation is what makes explicit teaching *possible*: without students' responses making their thinking visible, teachers 'cannot teach responsively because they are flying blind,' regardless of how well-designed the instruction is.

Participation and belonging are linked bidirectionally: disengagement from a few students damages collective classroom culture, just as a few dominant voices can crowd out a genuinely collaborative culture.

Her rehearsal argument: durable fluency (e.g., verb conjugation in a language class) requires sustained participation across many lessons over time - one or two rehearsals are 'utterly insufficient' for most students.

Her closing equity argument, the piece's sharpest claim: students who participate more receive disproportionately more feedback, corrective prompts, and encouragement - meaning the students who most need teacher support (who tend to participate least) are systematically the ones who receive the least of it.
quotes: Every teacher wants great participation from their students. But talk to any teacher, and they will tell you that participation is usually patchy.

It is students (not teachers) who need to wrestle with the content, concepts and skills of the curriculum... it is what students are thinking about that will likely determine the success of any lesson.
Put simply, if you're implementing any form of explicit teaching, great rates of student participation are not nice-to-have; they are a must-have.
With such limited evidence of learning, teachers cannot teach responsively because they are flying blind.

The kicker? Students who probably need the most from their teachers -- the most encouragement, the most frequent nods of support, the highest rates of corrective feedback -- are often the very students who give (and receive) the least.
Equitable student participation matters because participation opens doors for more.
